newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia plans 15 pct tax rebate on savings.
newsitem.headline: Australia plans 15 pct tax rebate on savings.

text.p: The Australian government said in its budget on Tuesday it planned to partly replace a planned tax cut known as the L-A-W tax cut with a 15 percent tax rebate on earnings from savings.

The savings tax rebate, which is estimated to cost A$2.04 billion a year by 2000/01 (July-June), would be introduced in two stages, with a 7.5 percent rebate applying from July 1, 1998 and the full rebate applying from July 1, 1999, after the election, due in the first half of 1999.
"The rebate will apply to the first A$3,000 of taxable income from savings, however derived," Treasurer Peter Costello said in his budget speech.
"The savings rebate takes the place of Labor's L-A-W tax cuts which were never paid," he said.

The former Labor government promised a series of tax cuts before the 1993 election, one of which was delivered while the other round was eventually replaced with a planned government contribution to superannuation schemes.

This second round L-A-W tax cut was forecast to cost up to A$3.98 billion a year by the year to June 30, 2001, so the savings tax rebate is effectively costing about a half of what the L-A-W tax cut would have cost.
The tax cut became known as the L-A-W tax cut after then Labor Prime Minister Paul Keating said the tax cut would happen because they were written into law and were: "L-A-W."
This effective reduction in the size of revenues lost to the tax cut is the main driver in the A$2.011 billion of annual budget improvements by 2000/01 announced in this 1997/98 budget.

The government announced it expected a A$3.853 billion underlying budget deficit for 1997/98, down from the A$6.856 billion forecast for the almost completed 1996/97 year, but well above market expectations of a A$2 billion underlying deficit because of lower than expected savings in 1997/98.
Costello said the rebate would apply to all types of savings, not just those put into superannuationm schemes.

"It is a significant encouragement to save in the form of superannuation, but it also provides assistance for individuals who are saving for other life cycle purposes such as education, health care, housing and retirement," Costello said.

The rebate means that banks in particular would effectively be able to offer a tax preferred method of savings to compete with savings put into superannuation funds -cles, after the government passed legislation this week allowing banks to set up retirement savings accounts (RSAs) which apply superannuation-like tax rules to bank account savings.
Although RSA savings must be kept in the account for use after retirement, savings eligible for the new tax rebate can be withdrawn and used for other purposes at any time.
Also on pensions and savings, the government announced it would legislate to maintain the pension at 25 percent of male total average weekly earnings.
This measure would cost an extra A$64 million in 1997/98, an extra A$450 million in 1998/99, A$700 million in 1999/00 and A$1.03 billion in 2000/01.
Costello also announced that from July 1998, people aged 65 and ready to receive the pension would be offered a bonus to keep working for another five years.
The bonus is calculated to be 9.4 percent of the basic pension entitlement for each year of pension deferral, up to a maximum of five years.
There would be a maximum bothus saving on pension payments.
It is expected to save A$42 million a year by 2000/01.
